title: Massacres That Shocked America Forever
fullText: Number one, Steven Paddock. The strangest thing about the aftermath was the silence he left behind. Not the silence of the desert or the silence of the emptied festival grounds along the Las Vegas strip. It was the silence inside the case itself, the missing motive, the missing note, the missing why. a wealthy retired accountant, a high limit gambler, a man with no criminal record and no known ideology, had planned one of the most methodical mass shootings in American history, then left investigators nothing to hold on to. That absence became the loudest thing about the entire tragedy, and it still shapes how the country talks about mass violence today. To understand the weight of what happened on the night of October 1st, 2017, you have to understand what the crime did to the systems around it. Las Vegas had always sold itself as a city of controlled chaos, noise, lights, crowds, cameras, security. The Route 91 Harvest Festival held across the street from the Mandandalay Bay Resort was a country music event of about 22,000 people. It was a familyfriendly openair venue. The kind of place families brought teenagers, off-duty nurses came to unwind, and couples traveled to for a long weekend. Within 11 minutes, that place became the deadliest single gunman shooting scene in modern American history. 60 people dead, more than 400 wounded by gunfire, and hundreds more injured in the panic. And the man responsible was not hiding in the crowd. He was above it on the 32nd floor, firing through two broken windows of a suite he had checked into days earlier. Steven Craig Paddock was 64 years old on the night of the attack. He had spent most of his life avoiding attention. He was born in 1953 in Iowa, the son of a mother who worked hard to raise her children in quiet stability, and a father, Benjamin Paddock, who lived a very different life. The elder Paddock was a bank robber who spent time on the FBI's most wanted list. Steven was still a small child when his father was arrested, and the family reinvented itself in the years afterward, changing locations, keeping the past out of view. Investigators who later combed through Paddock's history looked closely at this childhood, searching for a fracture point. They did not find the neat cinematic origin story that mass killings are often reduced to. What they found instead was a boy who grew up to be almost aggressively unremarkable. He worked as a mail carrier, then as an IRS agent, then in auditing roles for defense contractors. He was good with numbers. Colleagues remembered him as competent, cold, sometimes rude, but not menacing. In his 40s and 50s, he built modest wealth through real estate investments and later through highstakes video poker. He lived comfortably. He was known at casinos across Nevada and California. He tipped well. He drank. He argued with staff. He was, by most surface measurements, another anonymous high roller drifting through the machinery of the American gambling industry. The people closest to him described a man who had grown increasingly isolated in his final years. His long-term partner, who was out of the country during the attack, told investigators he had become obsessive, sometimes lying in bed moaning about things he never explained. His health had declined. He complained about pain. He had been prescribed medication for anxiety. He had lost significant amounts of money over the previous 2 years. and although he was still financially comfortable, his gambling patterns had shifted from disciplined to punishing. None of this on its own explained what he did, but taken together, it painted a portrait of a man quietly disintegrating in luxury hotel rooms while presenting the outside world with the same flat, unreadable face he had always worn. The planning began long before October. In the months leading up to the attack, Paddock purchased more than 30 firearms, mostly semi-automatic rifles. He bought thousands of rounds of ammunition. He researched other mass shootings. He booked hotel rooms overlooking major outdoor events in other cities, including a La Palooa festival in Chicago and a separate event in Las Vegas earlier that year, and then did not act. Investigators later concluded these were rehearsals or at least considerations. He was studying angles, sightelines, distances. He was studying the geometry of crowds. He was doing what he had done for a living for decades. He was auditing. On September 25th, 2017, he checked into a corner suite at the Mandalay Bay. Over the next several days, he brought in 22 firearms in luggage along with tools, ammunition, and cameras he intended to use to monitor the hallway outside his door. He rigged tripods for his rifles. He drilled a small hole into the door frame for surveillance. He arranged everything with the patience of a man who had all the time in the world. At 10:5 p.m. on October 1st, he began firing. The first burst came during a song by the country artist performing on stage that night. To the crowd below, the sound was confusing, a rattling, cracking noise that did not match anything they were expecting. Some people thought it was a technical malfunction. Some thought it was fireworks. Within seconds, the illusion collapsed. The gunfire kept coming, wave after wave, from an angle no one could immediately locate. Paddock had modified several rifles with devices known as bump stocks, which allowed semi-automatic weapons to fire at rates close to fully automatic. From the 32nd floor, that fire poured down onto a crowd with no cover, no exits, and no way to fight back. The attack lasted about 10 minutes. In that time, he fired more than a thousand rounds. When Las Vegas police officers finally reached the door of suite 32 to 135, they moved through hallways lit by muzzle flash smoke alarms and the scent of gunpowder. A security guard from the hotel, Jesus Campos, had already approached the floor after a separate alarm and had been shot through the door by Paddock, who had spotted him on his hallway cameras. That gunfire on the hallway, ironically, is believed by investigators to have interrupted Paddock's shooting rhythm and possibly ended the attack sooner than it otherwise might have. When SWAT breached the room, Paddock was already dead by his own hand. Then came the search for meaning, and it never quite arrived. Investigators went through his laptops, his phones, his financial records, his medical history, his relationships, his casino patterns, his gun purchases, and his travel. The FBI conducted one of the most extensive behavioral reviews in modern American criminal history. They interviewed his brothers, his partner, his doctors, his co-workers, casino employees, gun store clerks, and neighbors. And in the end, the official conclusion was almost unbearable in its plainness. There was no manifesto, no ideology, no religious motivation, no political message, no revenge target, no suicide note that explained the choice of venue or the choice of victims. The best supported theory investigators offered was that Paddock, aging, in decline, and increasingly obsessed with his own status and legacy, wanted to commit an act so large that it would guarantee his name would be remembered. He wanted notoriety, and he engineered a way to obtain it that would spare him the trial he did not want to sit through. Keep that detail in mind because it becomes far more important later. Not just in this case, but in the way America began to understand how a certain kind of quiet, methodical man can prepare a massacre without ever raising a flag. The aftermath rewrote parts of the country. Bump stocks, the device paddock used to increase his rate of fire, were banned at the federal level within a little over a year. The hotel industry o across Las Vegas and beyond overhauled do not disturb policies, room check policies, and internal surveillance protocols. Concert venues rebuilt their security perimeters. Country music communities held vigils that lasted for years. survivors filed civil lawsuits that eventually resulted in one of the largest hospitality settlements in US history with MGM Resorts agreeing to pay around $800 million to victims and families. The Mandandalay Bay itself renumbered its floors and the suite where the attack was planned no longer exists in the same form, but some pieces of the aftermath were quieter and heavier. Emergency responders spoke publicly for years afterward about what they carried home from Route 91. Nurses who had come to the festival as attendees became first responders in the middle of the gunfire. Offduty officers used their own belts as tourniquets. Strangers picked up strangers and ran. Truck drivers loaded wounded people into pickup beds and drove straight to the nearest hospitals. The number of lives saved that night by ordinary people cannot be precisely counted, but it is understood by investigators to have been in the hundreds. The families of the 60 who died continued the harder, longer work. Some formed advocacy groups. Some pushed for legislative changes. Some retreated entirely from public life. Vegas, a city built on forward motion, tried to move forward. But there is now a permanent memorial planned for the festival site. And there is a shared understanding among the people who lived through it that October 1st did not truly end on October 2nd. It kept unfolding through funerals, through hearings, through class action suits, through years of therapy, through anniversary vigils where the same country songs are played gently in the desert night. And there is the strangest legacy of all, the one investigators still discuss privately. Because Paddock left no explanation, the case has become a kind of mirror. Everyone who studies it sees something slightly different. The failure of financial monitoring, the failure of firearm regulation, the failure of hotel security, the failure of mental health outreach, the failure of the country, a man quietly reshaping himself into a weapon. His silence in a way forced the country to speak for him and the country has not stopped speaking about that night since. Steven Paddock was cremated. His remains were divided among family members. His name is rarely spoken aloud at memorials by design. Survivors and organizers made a conscious decision early on to avoid the trap of celebrity infamy to say the names of the 60 and not the name of the man on the 32nd floor. But his shadow still stretches over every open air concert in America. Every time a country act plays a stadium, someone in the crowd somewhere is thinking about exits. That is the residue he left. Not a message, not a movement, just a permanent tightening in the shoulders of a nation that used to feel safer under the stars. Number two, Adam Lanza. The town of New Town, Connecticut, was the kind of place people moved to, precisely so nothing would happen to them. It was quiet, wooded, expensive in an understated way, dotted with white churches and stone walls left over from colonial farms. On the morning of December 14th, 2012, that town became the site of a crime so incomprehensible that it changed the language of American politics, education, journalism, and grief. The person responsible was a 20-year-old who lived a few miles away in a house filled with locked rooms, unopened mail, and windows covered with black plastic bags. He had not been seen in public for months. He communicated with his own mother by email even though they lived in the same house. What Sandy Hook Elementary lost that morning, 21st grade children and six educators, became a wound the country has never fully closed. But the story of how the attack happened begins years earlier inside a family that outsiders assumed was thriving. Adam Peter Lanza was born in New Hampshire in 1992, the younger of two sons in a well-off family. His father worked as a tax executive at a major corporation. His mother, Nancy, was involved in her community, hosted holiday dinners, and drove her children to activities. Adam, from an early age, was described by teachers and pediatricians as sensitive, intelligent, and profoundly anxious. He struggled with sensory issues, disliked being touched, and had difficulty tolerating loud noises. He was later diagnosed with a range of conditions that included Asperger syndrome, obsessivecompulsive disorder, and severe anxiety. Those diagnosis on their own did not predict what came later. Millions of people carry those conditions and never harm anyone. But something else was moving underneath them, and it was moving in an environment that was not equipped to interrupt it. By his early teens, Adam's world had begun to shrink. His parents divorced. His older brother left for college. He and his mother moved into the new townhouse, a large colonial with more rooms than either of them used. He struggled at school, was pulled out of the mainstream classroom, and eventually completed his studies at home. His mother, by all accounts, tried. She read books on his conditions, consulted with therapists, adjusted his diet, protected him from sensory triggers. But she also tragically made choices that investigators later described as catastrophic misreadings of her son's inner state. She kept firearms in the house, believing that shared shooting range trips could give the two of them a rare point of connection. She trained him to use those weapons. She purchased ammunition. She stored some of the firearms unsecured. Inside his bedroom, Adam had built a private world that no one else was allowed to enter. The windows were blacked out. He had multiple computers. He wore earplugs, even indoors. He wrote long, detailed spreadsheets of past mass shootings, tracking the number of victims, the weapons used, the ages of the killers, and the response times of law enforcement. He communicated online with small communities of like-minded users who shared his fixation. He starved himself, dropping to a dangerous weight in the months before the attack. Investigators would later describe his room as the room of someone who had stopped being reachable. His mother at the time was researching new schools for him, considering a move to Washington State, telling friends that things were improving. She did not know what was in the spreadsheets. She did not know what was on the hard drives, which he later destroyed so completely that forensic teams could not fully recover them. On the morning of December 14th, he shot his mother while she was still in bed. Then he drove her car to Sandy Hook Elementary School wearing black clothing, carrying multiple weapons, and shot his way through the locked front entrance. The attack inside the school lasted less than 11 minutes. Investigators reconstructed his path through the building with the help of surveillance footage, staff statements, and physical evidence. He moved through two first grade Kong classrooms. The teachers in those rooms, Victoria and Marie, Lauren, Rachel, did everything they could. They pushed children into bathrooms, into closets, into corners. Some shielded students with their own bodies. The school's principal and school psychologist ran toward the sound of gunfire and were killed almost immediately. When police entered the building, Adam turned his weapon on himself. 20 children between the ages of six and seven were killed. Six adult staff members were killed. One first responder later said publicly that he could not describe what he saw and would not try because the families deserve to keep some part of that morning private. That principle, restraint, became a defining feature of how the Sandy Hook community would move forward. The investigation that followed was one of the most exhaustive ever conducted in Connecticut. The Office of the Child Advocate later produced a report that traced Adam's descent in painful detail. It documented years of missed intervention points, unadressed diagnosis, and a mother-son dynamic that had grown dangerously inshed. The report was careful not to blame any single individual. It focused instead on systemic gaps in mental health care, in school support, in family services, in firearms storage laws that had allowed a young man in profound crisis to plan and execute a mass shooting with weapons legally owned by a parent who did not understand the danger she was living with. His writings, recovered in fragments from damaged devices, revealed a person who had come to view himself as separate from the human species. He wrote about disgust with the world, disgust with himself, and a strange cold admiration for others who had committed similar attacks. He did not write a manifesto. He wrote something more disturbing, an incomplete map of a mind that had stopped negotiating with reality. Investigators concluded that his selection of an elementary school was tied to his fixation on other mass shootings and on a specific desire to commit an act that could not be surpassed in scale of horror. Beyond that, no clean motive emerged. There was no target grievance. There was no political message. There was no ideology. There was only a young man in a blacked out bedroom who had spent years disappearing into a fantasy of violence and finally acted on it. The aftermath in New Town became something the country had never fully seen before. Families of the children who died formed foundations one after another, each one carrying the name of a child. Some pushed for gun legislation. Some pushed for mental health reform. Some worked on school safety. Some devoted themselves to promoting kindness, literally building programs in schools to teach empathy, inclusion, and emotional literacy to young children. 26 lives had ended in that building, and out of them grew a scattered network of organizations that continues to operate more than a decade later. At the same time, the community endured something no one had anticipated. Conspiracy theorists, led most visibly by a radio personality who repeatedly claimed on air that the massacre had not happened, began harassing the families of the dead. Parents received death threats. Their addresses were published online. Some had to move. Some had to hire lawyers. Years later, defamation lawsuits filed by Sandy Hook families resulted in judgments totaling more than a billion dollars against that broadcaster and his companies. A legal outcome that reshaped how American courts would treat mass-cale disinformation about victims of tragedy. The school building itself was demolished. A new Sandy Hook Elementary was built on the same property, redesigned so that no child would enter the same physical space where the attack occurred. The design was quiet, careful, full of natural light. The Lanza house in New Town was also demolished at the request of the community, and the land where it once stood was returned to open space. Adam Lanza's name is rarely used at memorials. New Town, like Las Vegas, made a deliberate choice to center the victims. There is no marker for him, no grave visible to the public, no shrine. What remains publicly is the work of the families and the ongoing debate about how a country protects its children. A debate that intensified after Sandy Hook and has not resolved since. If this case feels impossible already, the next few names only make the pattern darker because what happened at Sandy Hook was not an isolated collapse. It was one of several attacks in which a young man built a private world of grievance and fantasy inside a bedroom, and no one outside that bedroom saw the shape of what was coming until it was already at the door. What haunts investigators most about Adam Lanza is not what he did in those 11 minutes. It is the years before them. The blacked out windows, the emails between mother and son inside the same house, the spreadsheets, the starvation, the silence, all of it visible in retrospect, but invisible in the moment because no one had a framework to see it clearly. New Town carries that lesson in a way no one wanted to be responsible for carrying. The children who died there would now be in their late teens. Their empty desks became the beginning of a national conversation that has never stopped even when the country has looked away. Number three, See Cho. The videos arrived by mail 2 days after the shooting sent to NBC News on the morning of the massacre from a post office in Blackburg, Virginia. Inside the package were photographs, a rambling video statement, and pages of writing. That mailing became, in a strange way, one of the most consequential single acts of self-branding in the history of American mass violence because it forced newsrooms across the world into make split-second decisions about what to show, what to withhold, and how much attention a killer's own postumous message deserved. Those decisions still shape newsroom policy today. But before the mailing, before the shooting, and before the campus of Virginia Tech became the site of the deadliest school shooting in American history at that time, there was a quiet young man who had spent almost his entire life not speaking. Sun Cho was born in South Korea in 1984 and moved to the United States with his family when he was 8 years old. His parents were hard-working, religious, and deeply concerned about the son who barely spoke, even inside their own home. Teachers in Northern Virginia, where the family settled, remembered him as a boy who could go entire school days without producing a single word. He was diagnosed in middle school with selective mutism and severe anxiety, and he received counseling for years. In high school, some of the intervention seemed to help. He was quiet but functional. He completed his coursework. He graduated. He was accepted to Virginia Tech, one of the largest universities in Virginia. Then, away from his family, the fragile scaffolding he had spent years building began to fail. At Virginia Tech, he became known to professors and roommates as unsettling in ways that were difficult to define. He rarely spoke in class. When he did speak, his voice was so low that other students strained to hear him. He wore sunglasses indoors. He photographed female classmates under desks without their knowledge. He wrote plays for creative writing courses that were so violent, so filled with rage and imagery of retaliation that one nationally known poet who taught in the program refused to have him in her class and warned the department that he was dangerous. she was overruled. He continued in the program. In late 2005, roughly a year and a half before the attack, several incidents brought him to the attention of campus police and mental health services. Two female students on separate occasions reported unwanted contact from him. A roommate, worried by comments Cho had made about suicide, contacted authorities. Cho was taken to a psychiatric facility, evaluated, and released with a recommendation for outpatient treatment. The evaluation described him as an imminent danger to himself. He did not follow up with the recommended care. There was no mechanism at that time to require him to. Virginia's laws on involuntary treatment, its systems for sharing mental health information across state agencies, and the university's ability to intervene were all limited in ways that would be re-examined intensely after the shooting. In the months that followed, he ordered firearms through the mail and from a local gun store, passing background checks that did not flag his psychiatric history because those records had not been transmitted to the federal database. He purchased ammunition, chains, and locks. He recorded video statements in his dorm room. He wrote the pages that would later be found in his mailing. On the morning of April 16th, 2007, he entered a dormatory building called West Amler Johnston Hall and killed two students on an upper floor. Campus authorities initially believed the shooting was a domestic incident and that the shooter had fled the area. Classes across campus continued. This assumption, later scrutinized in exhaustive detail by an independent review panel, became one of the most painful decision points of the entire tragedy. In the roughly 2 hours between that first shooting and the second, Cho returned to his dorm, mailed his package to NBC, and walked across campus carrying the weapons and ammunition he had prepared. He entered Norris Hall, an academic building. He chained several exterior doors shut from the inside. Then he moved through classrooms on the second floor. In roughly 9 minutes, he killed 30 additional people, students, and faculty across four classrooms before turning a weapon on himself. Among the dead was a professor named Livu Librescu, a Holocaust survivor in his 70s who held his classroom door closed with his body long enough for most of his students to escape through the windows. His story became one of many acts of quiet heroism from that morning that families and survivors continue to speak about. The response of investigators was immediate and enormous. State police, the FBI, and university administrators worked around the clock to reconstruct CHO's movements, purchases, communications, and mental state. What they built was a portrait of a young man whose interior life had been deteriorating for years in full view of a fragmented system. He had been evaluated. He had been reported. He had been flagged by professors. He had been the subject of concerned emails, hallway conversations, and campus police visits. And yet, the pieces had never come together in a single place where someone could act on all of them at once. The independent review panel appointed by the governor of Virginia produced a report that became a foundational document for how American universities approach threat assessment. It recommended coordinated behavioral intervention teams, groups that would bring together deans, campus police, mental health professionals of and residents life staff to share informations about students showing warning signs. It recommended reforms to Virginia's mental health commitment laws. It recommended changes to how federal background checks incorporated mental health data. Several of these recommendations were implemented at the federal level within a few years. Most universities in the United States now have some version of the behavioral intervention team that was built out of the lessons of Blackburg. The mailing to NBC and the network's decision to air portions of Chose video statements sparked a debate about media responsibility that has never fully settled. Some newsrooms decided that day that they would no longer name mass shooters or would name them only sparingly or would refuse to broadcast pre-recorded statements from perpetrators. Others argued that the public had a right to see the reality of what such a person looked like and said. The debate influenced coverage of every mass shooting that followed. It gave rise to campaigns such as the no notoriety movement in which survivors and journalists have pushed the focus to remain on victims rather than on the killer's carefully staged final performance. For Cho himself, the case ended in the classroom where he took his own life. There was no trial. There was no verdict. There was no explanation delivered under oath. What remained was the material he had prepared, the videos, the photographs, the writings, and the long patient work of the researchers who studied it to understand how a young man with severe untreated illness and access to firearms had turned a university campus into a killing field. Stay with the sequence because one overlooked clue changes the entire case. And in this instance, that clue was not a single object or a single missed report. It was the collective inability of many separate people in many separate offices to see that they were each holding a piece of the same picture. The families of the 32 victims formed foundations, scholarships, and advocacy groups. Some pushed for stricter background checks. Some worked in mental health outreach. Some devoted themselves to campus safety consulting. The university built a permanent memorial on the drill field at the center of campus. 32 stones of hokei limestone arranged in a gentle semicircle, each engraved with a single name. Students still leave flowers there on April 16th every year. The bell tolls 32 times Norris Hall was renovated. The classrooms where the shootings occurred were converted into a peace studies center. The building was not demolished but reshaped so that its future purpose could stand as a deliberate contrast to what had happened inside its walls. What lingers in the long aftermath is the way the Virginia Tech shooting reset the definition of what a campus threat looked like. Before Blackburg, university safety was largely designed around fire, weather, medical emergencies, and student conduct issues. After Blackburg, threat assessment became its own discipline, taught in graduate programs, studied at conferences, and integrated into the daily operations of nearly every large American university. The tragedy did not create the awareness that such attacks were possible, but it forced institutions to accept that ignoring the warning signs of a specific student over months and years could carry consequences no one could undo. Siong Huo was buried quietly. His family devastated largely withdrew from public life. His sister released a written statement of profound sorrow to the victim's families which many of them accepted with grace. His name is not carved into any memorial in Blackburg. The 32 names are. That too was a deliberate choice. A choice about who is remembered and by whom and what a community allows itself to say aloud when the wound number four. Omar Matin. The morning after the attack, the city of Orlando woke up to a version of itself it had never met. A community that had spent decades building safe nightlife spaces for LGBTQ residents. Spaces that had taken years of quiet, hard work was suddenly at the center of the deadliest attack on that community in American history at the time. The Pulse nightclub on South Orange Avenue was a place where people had first held hands in public, first come out, first felt at home. On June 12th, 2016, it became a crime scene that would take years to fully process, both physically and culturally. The man responsible was a 29-year-old security guard from Fort Pierce, Florida, whose life had been a long collision between grievance, instability, and an appetite for attention that he never quite knew how to satisfy. Omar Mir Sadi Matin was born in New York in 1986 to Afghan immigrant parents and grew up mostly in Florida. His father was a self-styled political figure who ran a cable access television program aimed at Afghan diaspora audiences and held opinions that alienated much of his own community. Omar's childhood was marked by multiple accounts from former classmates and teachers, by aggressive behavior, disciplinary problems, and a habit of playing at violence in ways that adults found disturbing even at the time. In middle school, he was reportedly ejected from a classroom for cheering after the September 11th attacks. He was suspended repeatedly. He was from a young age a boy who wanted people to look at him and did not care much whether they looked at him with admiration or fear. As an adult, that pattern continued. He attempted several careers. He briefly trained as a correctional officer before being dismissed. He worked as a security guard for a global private security company for years, which allowed him to legally carry firearms and gave him a professional identity he clung to. Cowworkers described him as volatile, prone to boasting, prone to racist and homophobic statements, and prone to sudden bursts of anger. He was married twice. His first wife left him after describing him as physically abusive and unstable. His second wife would later become the subject of her own federal trial. He came to the attention of the FBI twice before the attack in 2013 and 2014. In the first inquiry, co-workers reported that he had made claims about ties to multiple foreign terrorist organizations, claims that contradicted each other in ways investigators found strange. He was interviewed. He explained the statements as reactions to workplace harassment. The case was closed after months of surveillance produced no evidence of actual operational planning. In the second inquiry, his name surfaced in connection with a young man from Florida who had gone abroad to carry out a suicide bombing. Investigators again interviewed Matine. Again, no operational link was found. He was removed from active watch lists. In hindsight, those two closed investigations became one of the most debated aspects of the entire case. Some critics argued that the FBI should have kept him under surveillance. Others noted correctly that thousands of individuals are interviewed each year on the basis of similar tips and that continuing to monitor every closed case would be operationally impossible. What emerged in the years after was not a clear failure of any single agent but a broader question about how the country identifies the difference between a person who talks and a person who acts. Matine tragically was both. In the spring of 2016, he purchased a semi-automatic rifle and a handgun from a firearms store near his home. He passed the background checks. Because his prior FBI files had been closed, there was no flag to prevent the sale. In the weeks leading up to the attack, he visited Pulse and other Orlando nightclubs. According to some witnesses, visits that investigators later tried to reconstruct but could not fully verify given contradictory accounts. He researched other mass shootings. He watched extremist propaganda online. He posted messages on social media in the final hours before the attack expressing allegiance to a foreign terrorist organization. Allegiance that experts later described as opportunistic and shallow. cobbled together from several ideologically incompatible groups in a way that revealed he understood almost nothing about any of them. Just after 2:00 a.m. on June 12th, he entered pulse during Latin night, one of the busiest nights of the week. He opened fire. The attack lasted in its active phases several hours, though the majority of the deaths occurred in the opening minutes. He barricaded himself inside part of the club with hostages. He called 911 during the standoff and made a rambling statement about his motivations. He spoke with police negotiators. He claimed to have explosives. The Orlando Police Department, working with federal partners, made the decision to breach the wall of the club after determining that people inside were being actively killed and that further delay would cost more lives. In the final exchange of gunfire, Matine was killed. 49 people died at Pulse that night. Dozens more were wounded. The victims were overwhelmingly young, overwhelmingly Latino, and overwhelmingly members of the LGBTQ community. Their names, Amanda, Edward, Louise, Stanley, Kimberly, and many others became a roll call that would be read out at vigils in cities across the world in the days that followed. What happened next did not end with the arrest. Because there was no arrest, the shooter was dead, and the story of the crime became a story of what the country would do with what he had left behind. The investigation was one of the largest in FBI history. Agents reviewed his devices, his purchases, his workplace records, his family relationships, and his online activity. His widow was charged with aiding and abetting his provision of material support to a foreign terrorist organization and with obstruction of justice. She was acquitted at trial in 2018 after a jury concluded that prosecutors had not proven she knew of the attack in advance. That verdict itself became controversial and it highlighted a broader difficulty in the case. Matine appeared in the end to have acted alone in terms of planning and execution even as he wrapped his violence in borrowed ideological language. The Pulse nightclub building was never reopened. It was purchased for preservation with the intention of becoming a permanent memorial site. Plans for a formal memorial and museum went through years of proposals, disputes, and revisions, and the site has remained a place of ongoing community grief and community organizing. Every June, thousands gather there. Names are read, music plays. The legal and policy fallout was substantial. Florida did not pass sweeping firearm reforms in the immediate aftermath, but the state's response to a later school shooting was directly shaped by lessons drawn from Pulse. Nightclub security across the country was re-evaluated. LGBTQ advocacy organizations built new networks of trauma care, legal support, and safety training specifically designed for their communities. Blood donation policies, which at the time had prohibited many gay men from donating blood, including to the survivors of the attack, became the subject of intense public debate. And in the years afterward, those restrictions were eased, first partially and then more substantially. Matine himself has largely receded from public conversation, which is the outcome most survivors and families explicitly sought. What remains at the center of the pulse story is a community that refused to allow itself to be defined by the man who tried to destroy it. The 49 names are spoken, "His is not." Orlando adopted a phrase in the weeks after, "We will not let hate win," that appeared on murals, storefrs, city buses, and eventually a permanent installation near the Pulse site. What Pulse did to the country was not only to reveal again how much damage a single armed and untreated man could inflict. It also revealed how resilient a community could be when given no choice but to be resilient. The LGBTQ community in Central Florida did not disappear after that night. It grew louder. It grew more organized. It grew more visible in city politics, in state politics, and in national conversations. The people who died at Pulse became without ever choosing to be part of a movement that outlived the man who killed them. That in the end is the answer Omar Matine never expected. He wanted his name to matter. And a decade later in the city where he acted. The names that matter belong to the people who did not walk out of that building. Number five, Patrick Crus. Long before the sirens reached the parking lot of the Walmart near the Clo Vista Mall, on the morning of August 3rd, 2019, the city of El Paso had been quietly living as one of the safest large cities in the United States. It sat on the Texas Mexico border, home to a majority Hispanic population, deeply intertwined with its sister city of Sudarez, and known for decades of crossber family life, crossber commerce, and crossber identity. But there were signals even then that something was wrong beneath the surface. He was afraid of his father. He was ambivalent about the pressure to succeed. He carried a level of anxiety that he did not know how to name. He enlisted in the United States Marine Corps and served for several years, earning a scholarship that sent him to the University of Texas at Austin to study engineering. There his life began to fracture in ways that his outward appearance concealed for a long time. He struggled academically at first. He lost his scholarship. He returned to the Marines briefly. He came back to the University of Texas as a self-funded student. He married a young woman named Kathy. He held a series of jobs. He appeared to most people who knew him as an ambitious, personable, put together young man. But privately he was writing journal entries that revealed a growing sense of internal disorder. He complained of headaches. He complained of impulses he could not control. He worried about his own thoughts. In the spring of 1966, he sought help. He went to a university affiliated psychiatrist and in a single session described in stark terms his fear that he might one day climb the tower with a rifle and shoot people. The psychiatrist noted the statement in his file. He recommended followup. Wittmann did not return. There was at that time no mechanism by which such a statement made in a confidential clinical setting would have been relayed to anyone who could have prevented what came next. On the night of July 31st, 1966, Wittmann went to his mother's apartment in Austin and killed her. He returned to his own home and killed Cathy in her sleep. He left long handwritten notes explaining his actions in the language of someone trying in real time to make sense of what he was doing. He wrote that he wanted to spare his mother and his wife from what he called the embarrassment of what he intended to do the next day. He wrote that he could not fully explain the impulses driving him. He asked that his brain be examined after his death in case something could be learned from it. On the morning of August 1st, he assembled his equipment. He rented a dolly. He loaded a foot locker with rifles, a shotgun, handguns, ammunition, food, water, and personal items. He drove to the university. He rode the elevator up the tower carrying the equipment. He killed a receptionist on the observation deck and then from that height began firing on the campus below. For roughly the next hour and a half, the campus of the University of Texas became something almost unimaginable to the country of 1966. Students crawled behind low walls. Faculty carried the wounded away under fire. A newspaper photographer captured images that would appear in publications around the world. Local residents, in an improvisation that has been debated by historians ever since, arrived on the campus with their own hunting rifles and began firing at the observation deck to try to suppress Wittman's shooting. Two Austin police officers, along with a deputized civilian, eventually made their way up the tower, moved across the observation deck under fire and shot Wittmann at close range. The attack ended. The autopsy that followed produced one of the most discussed medical findings in the history of American criminal investigation. In accordance with Wittman's own request, his brain was examined. Pathologists discovered a tumor pressing against the amygdala, a region of the brain associated with the regulation of emotion and aggression. A commission appointed by the governor of Texas convened medical experts to consider whether the tumor might have contributed to Witman's behavior. The commission's report concluded with careful language that the tumor may have played a role in his conduct, but that its precise contribution could not be determined. That finding neither a clean exoneration nor a clean dismissal sparked a debate about the relationship between biology and violence that continues in academic literature to this day. The response to the shooting in terms of law enforcement was as consequential as the response to any single attack in modern American history. Police departments across the country recognized that they had no established protocol for a sustained attack by a heavily armed shooter operating from a fixed elevated position. In the years that followed, American SWAT teams, special weapons, and tactics units were formally developed and standardized, first in Los Angeles and then in departments across the country. The University of Texas tower shooting is one of the events most frequently cited as the operational trigger for the development of American SWAT. The tactical world we live in today in which every large American city has a specialized unit trained to respond to precisely this kind of attack has some of its earliest roots in the 96 minutes of that morning. The University of Texas tower itself remained standing and remained operational, though the observation deck was closed to the public for many years following the attack. Both because of concerns about copycat incidents and because of a broader institutional discomfort with the way the site had been used, it was reopened decades later with new security protocols, and it now operates as a controlled visitor space. A memorial garden was established on the campus in honor of the victims, unveiled in the late 1990s, more than three decades after the attack. That long delay itself became part of the story, a reflection of how uncomfortable the institution had been for a long time with publicly commemorating what had happened. Some of the survivors and family members spoke publicly for years afterward. Their accounts contributed to how researchers would come to understand the long tale of psychological injury following mass shootings. The way that trauma persists across decades. The way that anniversary reactions surface in unpredictable ways. The way that the physical spaces of the attack remain charged for the people who lived through them. That research in its way is also part of Wittman's legacy. Not because he intended it, but because the depth of the wound he inflicted forced the country to develop an academic and clinical vocabulary for that wound that had not existed before. Charles Wittmann is buried in Florida near his mother in a family plot. His name is often spoken in academic contexts where he is treated as a case study rather than as a figure to be memorialized. The University of Texas Memorial, when it was finally built, listed the names of the dead and did not name him. That choice, though made long before the more explicit notoriety movement of later decades, prefigured much of the ethical framework that later American communities would adopt in the aftermath of similar attacks. What the Texas Tower did to the country is difficult to summarize because it did so much. It gave American law enforcement a template for the specialized response unit. It gave American medicine a case study in the possible biological contributors to violent behavior. It gave American media its first extended live coverage of a mass shooting in progress. It gave American universities their first modern lesson in the vulnerability of open campuses. And it gave a generation of Americans an image. the tower, the smoke, the students crawling behind statues that would remain in the national memory long after the specific details of the attack had faded. More than half a century later, Austin has grown into a much larger city, and the university has grown around the tower. But every clear day, when the tower is lit for a graduation or an athletic victory, someone in the city looks up and remembers what once happened there. That remembrance, quiet and persistent, is one of the truest measurements of what the crime cost. Number 10, Howard Unra. Before the phrase mass shooting existed in the American vocabulary in anything like its current form, before news helicopters and live broadcasts and social media, there was a small residential block in Camden, New Jersey on the morning of September 6th, 1949 that became the site of what many historians and criminologists now consider the first modern single shooter mass killing in the United States. In 12 minutes, a 28-year-old World War II veteran named Howard Enrew walked out of his mother's apartment on River Road and killed 13 of his neighbors as he moved through the pharmacy, the tailor shop, the barbers, and the small businesses of his block. He did not run. He did not hide. He returned to his apartment afterward, waited for the police, and eventually surrendered without further violence. What he left behind was not only a shattered block of Camden, but also a case that would become foundational in the study of grievance-based violence in America. Enra had grown up in Camden, a workingclass industrial city across the Delaware River from Philadelphia. He was raised primarily by his mother in a household marked by financial strain and emotional distance. He was, by nearly all accounts of his early life, a quiet and religious young man. He was a churchgoer. He read the Bible extensively. He kept detailed diaries. He was described by neighbors as polite but withdrawn. He did not date. He had few close friends. He enlisted in the United States Army during the Second World War and served in Europe as a tank gunner. He saw combat. He kept meticulous notes in his personal journals about German soldiers he killed. He returned to Camden after the war and moved back into his mother's apartment. He enrolled briefly in pharmacy school under the GI Bill, then dropped out. He held only sporadic employment. He spent his days largely at home cleaning his firearms, reading, and increasingly keeping detailed lists of the neighbors he believed had wronged him. These lists became one of the most striking pieces of evidence in the aftermath of the shooting. When police entered his apartment, they found notebooks in which he had recorded grievances against specific neighbors, some real, some imagined. The tor next door had, in his account, insulted him. The pharmacist had shortchanged him. The cobbler had mocked him. A gate between his family's property and the neighboring house which the neighbor had built had become a fixation. In the days before the attack, that gate had been damaged, and Unrew believed the neighboring family was responsible. His notebooks contained the phrase retal, short for retaliation, next to certain names. He had in effect been building a private ledger of his intended violence for months and possibly years without anyone around him understanding what the entries meant. On the morning of September 6th, he walked out of his mother's apartment carrying a Luger pistol he had brought back from the war along with additional ammunition. He walked down the block calmly. He entered businesses one by one. He shot the cobbler in his shop. He shot the tailor. He shot the barber and tragically a small child who was in the barber's chair. He fired into passing cars. He shot children playing in the street. He shot people through their windows. In 12 minutes, 13 people were dead. Three more were wounded. He returned to his apartment. The Camden Police Department, arriving in force, surrounded the building. What followed became one of the most bizarre journalistic moments of the post-war era in American media. A reporter for a Philadelphia newspaper working the phones from the newsroom called the number for UNR's apartment. Unra extraordinarily picked up. The reporter identified himself. He asked Unrew questions. Unra calmly and briefly answered a few of them before saying he was too busy to talk because the police were shooting at him and hanging up. That short conversation was published almost immediately and remains one of the strangest documents of American crime reporting. Unra eventually surrendered to police after tear gas was deployed into the building. He was taken into custody. He was interviewed extensively over the following days. During those interviews, he gave the sentence that would define his case in the history of American criminology for generations to come. Asked why he had done what he did, he said with unnerving calm that he would have killed a thousand people if he had had bullets enough. That sentence in various forms has been quoted in virtually every serious study of grievance-based mass violence in the United States ever since. He was charged with murder, but he never went to trial. Courtappointed psychiatrists evaluated him and found that he was suffering from severe mental illness that rendered him incompetent to stand trial. He was committed to a state psychiatric hospital in New Jersey, the Trenton Psychiatric Hospital, where he would remain for the rest of his life. He lived in that facility for nearly six decades. He died there in 2009 at the age of 88. In all those years, he was not tried, was not convicted, and was not released. His case became one of the longest continuous psychiatric commitments in the history of American criminal justice. The impact of the Camden shooting on the developing field of American criminology and psychiatry was extensive, if slow, to unfold. In the immediate aftermath, the case was reported as a mass murder in the language of the time, and it was largely understood in the framework of a single deranged act rather than as an early example of a broader pattern. But as later mass shootings unfolded in the decades that followed at the Texas Tower, at the Sanedro McDonald's, at Lubie's cafeteria, and beyond, researchers began to return to the UNR case as a foundational precedent. his careful preparation, his private grievance lists, his selection of victims based on personal resentments rather than random encounter, his flat effect during and after the attack, his calm surrender, and his articulated wish to have killed more. All of these features would recur in variations in later cases. His shooting has been described in the academic literature as an early prototype of the pseudo commando attacker, a term developed by forensic psychiatrists decades later to describe grievancriven killers who plan their attacks with military precision. The block of River Road, where the attack took place, has since been transformed. The businesses Unrew entered are gone. The neighborhood itself changed in the decades that followed as Camden's economy shifted. There is no formal prominent memorial at the site. Camden, a city that in the second half of the 20th century faced significant hardships and social challenges, did not have the institutional bandwidth to build the kind of memorial architecture that later communities would erect after their own tragedies. What remains instead is the historical record, the police files, the newspaper archives, the psychiatric evaluations, the academic papers, and the oral histories of the families whose loved ones died that morning. Descendants of the victims still live in the region. Some have spoken publicly over the years about the long shadow of the attack on their families. Some have not. Unrew's psychiatric records became in the years leading up to and following his death one of the most studied case files in the field of American forensic psychiatry. Researchers had access to decades of clinical documentation. He was diagnosed and rediagnosed over the course of his commitment with a range of conditions including schizophrenia. He was interviewed periodically. He was by all accounts cooperative with the staff of the hospital where he lived. He did not in the more than half a century after his crimes publicly repudiate them or offer meaningful apology. He also did not by all available records express interest in being released. His name has largely faded from public consciousness in the United States. Younger generations of Americans who are familiar with the mass shootings of the modern era are frequently unaware that the earliest recognizable modern American mass shooting occurred in the year 1949 in a workingclass New Jersey neighborhood at the hands of a quiet young veteran with a Luger pistol and a notebook full of grievances. But among criminologists, forensic psychiatrists, and law enforcement analysts, the Camden shooting remains one of the essential reference points. It is one of the first cases studied in graduate programs on mass violence. It appears in the introductory chapters of textbooks on the subject. It is cited in FBI publications on threat assessment. Its lessons have quietly shaped the way the country understands the phenomenon it is still. decades later struggling to control. What Camden reveals looking back is that the pattern that has come to define the modern American mass shooting was already visible in fully formed shape by the middle of the 20th century. A young man in personal decline, a private ledger of resentments, a stockpile of firearms, a neighborhood chosen for its familiarity rather than its symbolism, a calm, deliberate walk through public spaces, a refusal to explain in any coherent political or ideological framework what had been done. All of it was there on that September morning in 1949, before the country had a vocabulary to describe what it was seeing. The names of the 13 who died that day are recorded in the Camden Historical Archives. They include a young child in a barber's chair. They include shopkeepers who had spent decades building small businesses on a modest street. They include people who had done nothing to Enra except live near him and be visible to him on the morning he chose to act. Their families carried that loss forward quietly without the national attention that later victims would receive. But the loss was no less real. And the case they became part of has shaped in ways most Americans do not realize the entire framework by which the country now studies prevents and responds to mass violence. That is the strange uncomfortable truth of the Howard Unrew case. It happened before the modern era of mass shootings began. And yet, in nearly every essential respect, it already was the modern era of mass shootings. The country would spend the next 75 years learning and relearning the lessons that were already visible on River Road on a September morning in 1949. That a man building a private catalog of grievances with access to firearms and no one around him equipped to see what he was doing can transform an ordinary block of an ordinary city into a wound that persists across generations. S.
fullTextVi: Số một, Steven Paddock. Điều kỳ lạ nhất sau đó là sự im lặng mà anh để lại. Không phải sự im lặng của sa mạc hay sự im lặng của sân lễ hội trống rỗng dọc theo dải Las Vegas. Đó là sự im lặng bên trong vụ án, động cơ còn thiếu, tờ ghi chú còn thiếu, thiếu tại sao. một kế toán viên đã nghỉ hưu giàu có, một tay cờ bạc giới hạn cao, một người đàn ông không có tiền án tiền sự và không có hệ tư tưởng nào được biết đến, đã lên kế hoạch cho một trong những vụ xả súng hàng loạt có phương pháp nhất ở Lịch sử nước Mỹ khi đó không để lại cho các nhà điều tra điều gì để bám víu. Sự vắng mặt đó đã trở thành điều ồn ào nhất trong toàn bộ thảm kịch, và nó vẫn định hình đất nước nói về bạo lực hàng loạt ngày nay như thế nào. Để hiểu được sức nặng của những gì đã xảy ra vào đêm ngày 1 tháng 10 năm 2017, bạn phải hiểu tội phạm đã làm gì với các hệ thống xung quanh nó. Las Vegas luôn tự cho mình là một thành phố của sự hỗn loạn, tiếng ồn, ánh sáng, đông người, camera, an ninh. Lễ hội Thu hoạch Tuyến 91 được tổ chức đối diện với Khu nghỉ dưỡng Vịnh Mandandalay là một sự kiện âm nhạc đồng quê với khoảng 22.000 người. Đó là một địa điểm ngoài trời thân thiện với gia đình. Loại nơi mà các gia đình đưa thanh thiếu niên đến, y tá ngoài giờ đến để thư giãn và các cặp đôi đi du lịch trong một ngày cuối tuần dài. Chỉ trong vòng 11 phút, nơi đó đã trở thành hiện trường vụ xả súng đẫm máu nhất thời hiện đại Lịch sử nước Mỹ. 60 người chết, hơn 400 người bị thương vì súng và hàng trăm người khác bị thương trong sự hoảng loạn. Và người chịu trách nhiệm không trốn trong đám đông. Anh ta ở trên nó trên tầng 32, bắn xuyên qua hai cửa sổ vỡ của một căn phòng mà anh ấy đã thuê vài ngày trước đó. Steven Craig Paddock đã 64 tuổi vào đêm xảy ra vụ tấn công. Anh ấy đã dành phần lớn cuộc đời mình để tránh sự chú ý. Ông sinh năm 1953 tại Iowa, là con trai của một người mẹ làm nghề vất vả nuôi dạy những đứa con của mình trong sự ổn định thầm lặng, và một người cha, Benjamin Paddock, người đã sống một cuộc sống rất khác. Paddock lớn tuổi là một tên cướp ngân hàng từng làm việc cho FBI nhiều nhất danh sách truy nã. Steven vẫn còn là một đứa trẻ nhỏ khi cha anh và gia đình bị bắt đã tự tái tạo lại chính mình trong những năm sau đó, thay đổi địa điểm, giữ kín quá khứ. Các nhà điều tra sau này tìm hiểu lịch sử của Paddock đã xem xét kỹ thời thơ ấu này và tìm kiếm một điểm gãy. Họ không tìm thấy câu chuyện có nguồn gốc điện ảnh gọn gàng mà những vụ giết người hàng loạt thường xảy ra giảm xuống. Thay vào đó, những gì họ tìm thấy là một cậu bé lớn lên gần như hung hãn không đáng kể. Anh ấy làm người vận chuyển thư, sau đó là đại lý IRS, sau đó làm kiểm toán vai trò của các nhà thầu quốc phòng Anh ấy giỏi về các con số. Các đồng nghiệp nhớ đến anh là người có năng lực, lạnh lùng, đôi khi thô lỗ nhưng không đáng sợ. Ở độ tuổi 40 và 50, ông đã tạo dựng được khối tài sản khiêm tốn thông qua đầu tư bất động sản và sau đó thông qua video poker đặt cược cao. Anh sống thoải mái. Anh ta được biết đến ở các sòng bạc trên khắp Nevada và California. Anh ấy boa tốt. Anh ấy đã uống. Anh ta tranh cãi với nhân viên. Theo hầu hết các phép đo bề mặt, anh ta là một con lăn cao ẩn danh khác đang trôi qua máy móc của ngành công nghiệp cờ bạc Mỹ. Những người gần gũi nhất với anh ấy mô tả một người đàn ông ngày càng bị cô lập trong những năm cuối đời của ông. Đối tác lâu năm của anh ta, người đã ở nước ngoài trong vụ tấn công, đã nói với các nhà điều tra anh đã trở nên ám ảnh, đôi khi nằm trên giường rên rỉ về những điều anh chưa bao giờ giải thích. Sức khỏe của ông đã giảm sút. Anh ấy phàn nàn về sự đau đớn. Anh ấy đã được kê đơn thuốc vì lo lắng. Anh ta đã mất một số tiền đáng kể trong 2 năm trước đó. và mặc dù anh ta vẫn thoải mái về mặt tài chính, nhưng hình thức cờ bạc của anh ta đã chuyển từ kỷ luật sang một bên. để trừng phạt. Bản thân những điều này không giải thích được việc anh ấy đã làm, nhưng gộp lại, nó vẽ chân dung một người đàn ông lặng lẽ tan rã trong phòng khách sạn sang trọng khi trình bày thế giới bên ngoài với khuôn mặt phẳng lặng, khó hiểu mà anh luôn mang. Việc lập kế hoạch đã bắt đầu từ lâu trước tháng 10. Trong những tháng trước vụ tấn công, Paddock đã mua hơn 30 khẩu súng, chủ yếu là súng trường bán tự động. Anh ta đã mua hàng nghìn viên đạn. Ông nghiên cứu các vụ xả súng hàng loạt khác. Anh ấy đặt phòng khách sạn nhìn ra các sự kiện ngoài trời lớn ở các thành phố khác, bao gồm cả La Lễ hội Palooa ở Chicago và một sự kiện riêng ở Las Vegas vào đầu năm đó, rồi không hành động. Các nhà điều tra sau đó kết luận đây chỉ là những cuộc diễn tập hoặc ít nhất là những sự cân nhắc. Anh ấy đang nghiên cứu các góc, đường ngắm, khoảng cách. Anh ấy đang nghiên cứu hình học của đám đông. Anh ấy đang làm những gì anh ấy đã làm để kiếm sống trong nhiều thập kỷ. Anh ấy đang kiểm toán. Vào ngày 25 tháng 9 năm 2017, anh ấy đã nhận phòng ở căn góc ở Vịnh Mandalay. Trong vài ngày tiếp theo, anh ta mang theo 22 khẩu súng trong hành lý cùng với công cụ, đạn dược và máy ảnh mà anh định sử dụng để giám sát hành lang bên ngoài cửa. Anh ta lắp đặt giá ba chân cho súng trường của mình. Anh khoan một lỗ nhỏ trên khung cửa để giám sát. Anh sắp xếp mọi việc với sự kiên nhẫn của một người có tất cả thời gian trên thế giới. Lúc 10:5 chiều. m. vào ngày 1 tháng 10, anh ta bắt đầu nổ súng. Vụ nổ đầu tiên xảy ra trong một bài hát của nghệ sĩ đồng quê biểu diễn trên sân khấu đêm đó. Đối với đám đông bên dưới, âm thanh đó thật khó hiểu, một tiếng lạch cạch, răng rắc không phù hợp với bất cứ điều gì họ mong đợi. Một số người cho rằng đó là trục trặc kỹ thuật. Một số người cho rằng đó là pháo hoa. Trong vòng vài giây, ảo ảnh sụp đổ. Tiếng súng cứ dồn dập, hết đợt này đến đợt khác, từ một góc độ không ai có thể ngay lập tức định vị. Paddock đã sửa đổi một số súng trường với thiết bị được gọi là báng súng, cho phép bán tự động vũ khí bắn ở tốc độ gần như hoàn toàn tự động. Từ tầng 32, ngọn lửa đó trút xuống đám đông không có chỗ che chắn, không có lối thoát và không có cách nào để chống trả. Cuộc tấn công kéo dài khoảng 10 phút. Trong thời gian đó, anh đã bắn hơn một nghìn viên đạn. Khi các sĩ quan cảnh sát Las Vegas cuối cùng cũng tới được cửa phòng từ phòng 32 đến phòng 135, họ di chuyển qua các hành lang được thắp sáng bởi chuông báo khói nhấp nháy ở đầu nòng và mùi thuốc súng. Trước khi cụm từ xả súng hàng loạt tồn tại trong từ vựng của người Mỹ ở bất cứ thứ gì giống như hình thức hiện tại, trước khi có máy bay trực thăng tin tức, chương trình phát sóng trực tiếp và phương tiện truyền thông xã hội, đã có khu dân cư nhỏ ở Camden, New Jersey vào sáng ngày 6 tháng 9 năm 1949 đã trở thành địa điểm mà nhiều nhà sử học và nhà tội phạm học ngày nay coi là đầu tiên vụ giết người hàng loạt bằng game bắn súng hiện đại ở Hoa Kỳ. Trong 12 phút, một cựu chiến binh Thế chiến thứ hai 28 tuổi tên Howard Enrew bước ra căn hộ của mẹ anh trên đường River và giết chết 13 người hàng xóm của anh anh ấy di chuyển qua hiệu thuốc, tiệm may, thợ cắt tóc và các cơ sở kinh doanh nhỏ khối của anh ấy. Anh ấy không chạy. Anh ấy không giấu giếm. Sau đó anh ta trở về căn hộ của mình, đợi cảnh sát và cuối cùng đầu hàng mà không có thêm bạo lực. Những gì anh ta để lại không chỉ là một khối Camden vỡ vụn mà còn cả một trường hợp sẽ trở thành nền tảng trong việc nghiên cứu bạo lực dựa trên khiếu nại ở Mỹ. Enra lớn lên ở Camden, một thành phố công nghiệp của tầng lớp lao động bên kia sông Delaware từ Philadelphia. Anh chủ yếu được mẹ nuôi dưỡng trong một gia đình gặp khó khăn về tài chính và khoảng cách tình cảm. Theo hầu hết các ghi chép về thời kỳ đầu đời của mình, ông là một người trầm lặng và sùng đạo chàng trai trẻ. Anh ấy là một người đi nhà thờ. Ông đọc Kinh thánh rất nhiều. Anh ấy ghi nhật ký chi tiết. Anh ta được hàng xóm mô tả là người lịch sự nhưng rút lui. Anh ấy không hẹn hò. Anh ấy có rất ít bạn thân. Ông gia nhập Quân đội Hoa Kỳ trong Thế chiến thứ hai và phục vụ ở châu Âu với tư cách là một xạ thủ xe tăng. Anh ta đã nhìn thấy chiến đấu. Ông ghi chép tỉ mỉ trong nhật ký cá nhân về những người lính Đức mà ông đã giết. Anh trở lại Camden sau chiến tranh và chuyển về căn hộ của mẹ mình. Anh ấy đăng ký một thời gian ngắn vào trường dược theo GI Bill, sau đó bỏ học. Anh ta chỉ làm việc lẻ tẻ. Anh ấy dành phần lớn thời gian ở nhà để lau súng, đọc sách và ngày càng giữ danh sách chi tiết những người hàng xóm mà anh tin rằng đã đối xử sai trái với anh. Những danh sách này đã trở thành một trong những bằng chứng nổi bật nhất sau đó của vụ nổ súng. Khi cảnh sát ập vào căn hộ của anh, họ tìm thấy cuốn sổ ghi những lời than phiền của anh chống lại những người hàng xóm cụ thể, một số có thật, một số tưởng tượng. Theo lời kể của anh ta, người ở nhà bên cạnh đã xúc phạm anh ta. Dược sĩ đã đổi chỗ cho anh ta. Người thợ giày đã chế nhạo anh ta. Cánh cổng nối đất của gia đình anh với nhà hàng xóm được xây dựng đã trở thành một điểm cố định. Những ngày trước cuộc tấn công, cánh cổng đó đã bị hư hại và Unrew tin rằng gia đình hàng xóm phải chịu trách nhiệm. Trong sổ ghi chép của ông có cụm từ retal, viết tắt của sự trả thù, bên cạnh một số cái tên. Trên thực tế, anh ta đã xây dựng một sổ cái riêng về hành vi bạo lực dự định của mình dành cho nhiều tháng và có thể nhiều năm mà không có ai xung quanh anh ấy hiểu được ý nghĩa của các mục đó. Sáng ngày 6/9, anh bước ra khỏi căn hộ của mẹ mình mang theo một khẩu súng lục Luger mà anh ta mang về từ chiến tranh cùng với nhiều đạn dược bổ sung. Anh ấy bước xuống khu nhà một cách bình tĩnh. Anh bước vào từng doanh nghiệp một. Anh ta bắn người thợ giày trong cửa hàng của mình. Anh ta bắn người thợ may. Anh ta bắn người thợ cắt tóc và bi kịch là một đứa trẻ nhỏ đang ở trong tiệm cắt tóc cái ghế. Anh ta bắn vào những chiếc ô tô đi qua. Anh ta bắn những đứa trẻ đang chơi trên đường phố. Anh ta bắn mọi người qua cửa sổ của họ. Trong 12 phút, 13 người đã chết. Ba người nữa bị thương. Anh trở về căn hộ của mình. Sở cảnh sát Camden có mặt, bao vây tòa nhà. Những gì diễn ra sau đó đã trở thành một trong những khoảnh khắc báo chí kỳ lạ nhất thời hậu chiến trên truyền thông Mỹ. Một phóng viên của một tờ báo ở Philadelphia đang sử dụng điện thoại từ phòng tin tức gọi là số căn hộ của UNR. Unra đã nhặt được một cách bất thường. Phóng viên đã tự nhận diện. Anh ấy hỏi Unrew những câu hỏi. Unra bình tĩnh và trả lời ngắn gọn một vài câu trước khi nói rằng anh ấy cũng vậy bận nói chuyện vì cảnh sát đã bắn anh ta và cúp máy. Đoạn hội thoại ngắn đó gần như được công bố ngay lập tức và vẫn là một trong những tài liệu kỳ lạ nhất báo cáo tội phạm của Mỹ. Unra cuối cùng đã đầu hàng cảnh sát sau khi hơi cay được triển khai vào tòa nhà. Anh ta đã bị bắt giam. Anh ấy đã được phỏng vấn rộng rãi trong những ngày tiếp theo. Trong những cuộc phỏng vấn đó, anh ấy đã đưa ra câu xác định trường hợp của mình trong lịch sử tội phạm học Mỹ cho các thế hệ mai sau. Khi được hỏi tại sao lại làm như vậy, anh ấy nói với vẻ bình tĩnh đến đáng sợ rằng anh ta sẽ giết cả nghìn người nếu có đủ đạn. Câu đó dưới nhiều hình thức khác nhau đã được trích dẫn trong hầu hết mọi nghiên cứu nghiêm túc về bạo lực hàng loạt dựa trên khiếu nại ở Hoa Kỳ kể từ đó. Anh ta bị buộc tội giết người, nhưng anh ta không bao giờ ra tòa. Các bác sĩ tâm thần được tòa án chỉ định đã đánh giá anh ta và phát hiện ra rằng anh ta đang mắc bệnh tâm thần nặng điều đó khiến anh ta không đủ năng lực để hầu tòa. Anh ta được đưa vào bệnh viện tâm thần tiểu bang ở New Jersey, Bệnh viện Tâm thần Trenton Bệnh viện, nơi anh sẽ gắn bó suốt đời. Ông đã sống ở cơ sở đó gần sáu thập kỷ. Ông qua đời ở đó năm 2009, thọ 88 tuổi. Trong ngần ấy năm, anh ta không bị xét xử, không bị kết án và không bị phát hành. Vụ án của anh ta đã trở thành một trong những cam kết tâm thần liên tục dài nhất trong lịch sử Tư pháp hình sự Mỹ. Tác động của vụ xả súng ở Camden đối với lĩnh vực tội phạm học đang phát triển của Mỹ và tâm thần học đã được mở rộng, mặc dù chậm. Ngay sau đó, vụ án được báo cáo là một vụ giết người hàng loạt tại ngôn ngữ của thời đó, và nó phần lớn được hiểu trong khuôn khổ của hành động loạn trí đơn lẻ chứ không phải là một ví dụ ban đầu của một mô hình rộng hơn. Nhưng sau đó, các vụ xả súng hàng loạt diễn ra trong những thập kỷ sau đó tại Texas Tower, tại Sanedro McDonald's, tại căng tin của Lubie và xa hơn nữa, các nhà nghiên cứu bắt đầu quay trở lại lấy trường hợp UNR làm tiền lệ nền tảng. sự chuẩn bị kỹ lưỡng của anh ấy, danh sách khiếu nại riêng tư của anh ấy, việc anh ấy lựa chọn nạn nhân dựa trên cá nhân sự oán giận hơn là cuộc gặp gỡ ngẫu nhiên, hiệu ứng phẳng của anh ta trong và sau cuộc tấn công, của anh ta bình tĩnh đầu hàng và mong muốn được giết nhiều hơn. Tất cả các tính năng này sẽ tái diễn với nhiều biến thể trong các trường hợp sau này. Cú bắn của anh ta đã được mô tả trong tài liệu học thuật như một nguyên mẫu ban đầu của kẻ tấn công đặc công giả, một thuật ngữ được các bác sĩ tâm thần pháp y phát triển nhiều thập kỷ sau để mô tả những kẻ sát nhân đau buồn lên kế hoạch tấn công với độ chính xác quân sự. Đoạn đường River, nơi xảy ra vụ tấn công, đã được chuyển đổi. Các doanh nghiệp Unrew tham gia đã biến mất. Bản thân khu vực lân cận đã thay đổi trong những thập kỷ sau đó khi nền kinh tế của Camden thay đổi. Không có đài tưởng niệm nổi bật chính thức tại địa điểm này. Camden, một thành phố vào nửa sau thế kỷ 20 phải đối mặt với khó khăn và thách thức xã hội, không có đủ băng thông thể chế để xây dựng loại hình về kiến ​​trúc tưởng niệm mà các cộng đồng sau này sẽ dựng lên sau thảm kịch của chính họ. Thay vào đó, những gì còn lại là hồ sơ lịch sử, hồ sơ của cảnh sát, kho lưu trữ báo chí, đánh giá tâm thần, các bài báo học thuật và lịch sử truyền miệng của những gia đình có người thân những người đã chết vào sáng hôm đó. Con cháu của các nạn nhân vẫn sinh sống trong vùng. Một số người đã lên tiếng công khai trong nhiều năm về cái bóng lâu dài của vụ tấn công về gia đình họ. Một số thì không. Hồ sơ tâm thần của Unrew được lưu giữ trong những năm trước và sau khi ông qua đời một trong những hồ sơ vụ án được nghiên cứu nhiều nhất trong lĩnh vực tâm thần pháp y của Mỹ. Các nhà nghiên cứu đã có quyền truy cập vào tài liệu lâm sàng trong nhiều thập kỷ. Anh ấy đã được chẩn đoán và chẩn đoán lại trong quá trình cam kết của mình với phạm vi của các tình trạng bao gồm cả bệnh tâm thần phân liệt. Ông đã được phỏng vấn định kỳ. Về mọi mặt, anh ấy luôn hợp tác với các nhân viên của bệnh viện nơi anh ấy đã sống. Anh ta đã không làm vậy trong hơn nửa thế kỷ sau khi tội ác của mình được công khai từ chối họ hoặc đưa ra lời xin lỗi có ý nghĩa. Theo tất cả hồ sơ hiện có, anh ta cũng không bày tỏ sự quan tâm đến việc được trả tự do. Tên của ông phần lớn đã mờ nhạt khỏi ý thức của công chúng ở Hoa Kỳ. Thế hệ trẻ người Mỹ đã quen với những vụ xả súng hàng loạt thời hiện đại mọi người thường không biết rằng vụ xả súng hàng loạt hiện đại sớm nhất ở Mỹ đã xảy ra ở năm 1949 tại một khu dân cư thuộc tầng lớp lao động ở New Jersey dưới bàn tay của cựu chiến binh trẻ trầm tính với khẩu súng lục Luger và cuốn sổ đầy bất bình. Nhưng trong số các nhà tội phạm học, bác sĩ tâm thần pháp y và các nhà phân tích thực thi pháp luật, vụ xả súng ở Camden vẫn là một trong số các điểm tham chiếu thiết yếu. Đây là một trong những trường hợp đầu tiên được nghiên cứu trong chương trình sau đại học về bạo lực hàng loạt. Nó xuất hiện trong các chương giới thiệu của sách giáo khoa về chủ đề này. Nó được trích dẫn trong các ấn phẩm của FBI về đánh giá mối đe dọa. Những bài học của nó đã âm thầm định hình cách đất nước hiểu về hiện tượng này vẫn. nhiều thập kỷ sau đấu tranh để kiểm soát. Điều mà Camden tiết lộ khi nhìn lại là mô hình đã được xác định vụ xả súng hàng loạt hiện đại của Mỹ đã được hiển thị dưới dạng hoàn chỉnh bởi giữa thế kỷ 20. Một thanh niên sa sút cá nhân, một cuốn sổ riêng ghi những oán hận, một kho dự trữ súng ống, một khu phố được chọn vì sự quen thuộc hơn là tính biểu tượng của nó, một điềm tĩnh, có chủ ý đi bộ qua không gian công cộng, từ chối giải thích bằng bất kỳ ý thức hệ chính trị hoặc ý thức hệ mạch lạc nào khuôn khổ những gì đã được thực hiện. Tất cả đều có mặt vào buổi sáng tháng 9 năm 1949 đó, trước đất nước có vốn từ vựng để mô tả những gì nó đang nhìn thấy. Tên của 13 người thiệt mạng ngày hôm đó được ghi trong Camden Lưu trữ lịch sử. Họ bao gồm một đứa trẻ ngồi trên ghế cắt tóc. Họ bao gồm những chủ cửa hàng đã dành hàng thập kỷ để xây dựng cơ sở kinh doanh nhỏ trên một con phố khiêm tốn. Họ bao gồm những người chưa từng làm gì Enra ngoại trừ việc sống gần anh ta và được nhìn thấy anh ấy vào buổi sáng anh ấy chọn hành động. Gia đình họ lặng lẽ gánh chịu sự mất mát đó mà không có sự quan tâm của cả nước như những nạn nhân sau này sẽ nhận được. Nhưng sự mất mát cũng không kém phần thực tế. Và vụ án mà họ tham gia đã định hình theo cách mà hầu hết người Mỹ làm chưa nhận ra toàn bộ khuôn khổ mà đất nước hiện đang nghiên cứu ngăn ngừa và ứng phó đến bạo lực hàng loạt. Đó chính là sự thật khó chịu đến lạ lùng của vụ Howard Unrew. Nó xảy ra trước khi kỷ nguyên xả súng hàng loạt hiện đại bắt đầu. Tuy nhiên, ở hầu hết mọi khía cạnh thiết yếu, đó đã là kỷ nguyên hiện đại của vụ xả súng hàng loạt. Đất nước sẽ dành 75 năm tiếp theo để học đi học lại những bài học đã xuất hiện trên đường River vào một buổi sáng tháng 9 năm 1949. Rằng một người đàn ông đang xây dựng một danh mục khiếu nại riêng về quyền tiếp cận súng ống và không ai xung quanh anh ta được trang bị để xem những gì anh ta đang làm có thể biến đổi khối nhà bình thường của một thành phố bình thường thành một vết thương dai dẳng qua nhiều thế hệ. S.
